Text: The {{c1::Collections Framework}} is a unified architecture representing and manipulating collections, including interfaces, implementations, and algorithms.
Extra:
Why it matters: It reduces programming effort, increases performance, and fosters software reuse by providing standard data structures.

Details: The Collections Framework consists of three parts: interfaces, implementations, and algorithms. Note that Map does NOT extend Collection.

Text: The Collections Framework consists of three main parts: {{c1::interfaces}}, {{c2::implementations}}, and {{c3::algorithms}}.
Extra:
Gotcha: Assuming all collections extend the Collection interface, whereas Map is a completely separate hierarchy.

Details: The Collections Framework consists of three parts: interfaces, implementations, and algorithms. Note that Map does NOT extend Collection.

Text: The root traversal contract in Java that returns an Iterator and enables for-each loop traversal is {{c1::Iterable}}.
Extra:
Why it matters: It provides a standard way to obtain an Iterator for sequential traversal.

Details: Requires implementing iterator(). Example:
for(String s : list) { ... }
Gotcha: Modifying the collection during traversal throws ConcurrentModificationException.

Text: Any class that implements the {{c1::Iterable}} interface must provide an implementation for the {{c2::iterator()}} method.
Extra:
Gotcha: Modifying the collection directly inside an enhanced for loop, causing a ConcurrentModificationException.

Details: Requires implementing iterator(). Example:
for(String s : list) { ... }
Gotcha: Modifying the collection during traversal throws ConcurrentModificationException.

Text: The root interface of the main collection hierarchy is {{c1::Collection}}.
Extra:
Why it matters: Defines common operations like size(), isEmpty(), contains(), add(), and remove() shared by all collections.

Details: Root of List, Set, Queue hierarchies. Common methods: size(), add(), remove(). Note that Map does not extend Collection.

Text: The {{c1::Collection}} interface is extended by {{c2::List}}, {{c3::Set}}, and {{c4::Queue}}.
Extra:
Gotcha: Assuming Map extends Collection (it does not) or that Collection guarantees a specific order.

Details: Root of List, Set, Queue hierarchies. Common methods: size(), add(), remove(). Note that Map does not extend Collection.

Text: An ordered collection that can contain duplicate elements and supports index-based access is {{c1::List}}.
Extra:
Why it matters: Essential when element order must be preserved and duplicate values are permitted.

Details: Ordered collection, duplicate-friendly. Backed by array (ArrayList) or nodes (LinkedList). Positional access via get(index).

Text: Common implementations of the List interface include {{c1::ArrayList}} and {{c2::LinkedList}}.
Extra:
Gotcha: Using index-based deletion in a forward loop, which shifts elements and causes items to be skipped.

Details: Ordered collection, duplicate-friendly. Backed by array (ArrayList) or nodes (LinkedList). Positional access via get(index).

Text: A collection that cannot contain duplicate elements is {{c1::Set}}.
Extra:
Why it matters: Ensures uniqueness of entries automatically using equality checks.

Details: No duplicates. HashSet has O(1) ops (unordered); TreeSet has O(log N) ops (sorted). Rejection based on equals/hashCode or compareTo.

Text: The three main implementations of the Set interface are {{c1::HashSet}}, {{c2::LinkedHashSet}}, and {{c3::TreeSet}}.
Extra:
Gotcha: Modifying key fields of an object after adding it to a HashSet, making the object unretrievable.

Details: No duplicates. HashSet has O(1) ops (unordered); TreeSet has O(log N) ops (sorted). Rejection based on equals/hashCode or compareTo.

Text: A collection designed for holding elements prior to processing, typically in FIFO order, is {{c1::Queue}}.
Extra:
Why it matters: Decouples producers from consumers in processing pipelines using standard queue APIs.

Details: Typically FIFO. Inserters: offer() vs add(); Removers: poll() vs remove(); Peepers: peek() vs element().

Text: Queue methods that return special values on failure instead of throwing exceptions are {{c1::offer()}}, {{c2::poll()}}, and {{c3::peek()}}.
Extra:
Gotcha: Confusing exception-throwing methods (add, remove) with special-value return methods (offer, poll).

Details: Typically FIFO. Inserters: offer() vs add(); Removers: poll() vs remove(); Peepers: peek() vs element().

Text: A double-ended queue that supports element insertion and removal at both ends is {{c1::Deque}}.
Extra:
Why it matters: Can be used as both a FIFO queue and a LIFO stack. ArrayDeque is faster than Stack and LinkedList.

Details: Double-ended queue. Useful as stack (push, pop) or queue (addLast, removeFirst). ArrayDeque is the default choice.

Text: To implement a stack, Deque provides the LIFO methods {{c1::push()}} and {{c2::pop()}}.
Extra:
Gotcha: Using legacy Stack instead of Deque for stack operations, incurring synchronization overhead.

Details: Double-ended queue. Useful as stack (push, pop) or queue (addLast, removeFirst). ArrayDeque is the default choice.

Text: An object that maps keys to values and cannot contain duplicate keys is {{c1::Map}}.
Extra:
Why it matters: Enables key-value associations and fast key-based retrieval.

Details: Key-value pairs. Keys must be unique. HashMap (unordered), LinkedHashMap (insertion/access order), TreeMap (sorted).

Text: Although part of the Collections Framework, the {{c1::Map}} interface does NOT extend the {{c2::Collection}} interface.
Extra:
Gotcha: Expecting Map to implement Collection, or using mutable objects as keys and changing their hashCode.

Details: Key-value pairs. Keys must be unique. HashMap (unordered), LinkedHashMap (insertion/access order), TreeMap (sorted).

Text: A resizable-array implementation of the List interface is {{c1::ArrayList}}.
Extra:
Why it matters: Provides O(1) random access and low memory overhead, making it the default choice for lists.

Details: Backed by array. Growth is usually 1.5x of old capacity using System.arraycopy(). O(1) random access, O(N) middle insert/delete.

Text: ArrayList provides {{c1::O(1)}} random access time complexity, but middle insertions take {{c2::O(N)}} time due to element shifting.
Extra:
Gotcha: Adding/removing items in the middle of a large ArrayList frequently, incurring O(N) element shifting cost.

Details: Backed by array. Growth is usually 1.5x of old capacity using System.arraycopy(). O(1) random access, O(N) middle insert/delete.

Text: A doubly-linked list implementation of the List and Deque interfaces is {{c1::LinkedList}}.
Extra:
Why it matters: Permits O(1) insertion/removal at the head and tail without resizing overhead.

Details: Backed by doubly-linked nodes (3 references per node: value, next, prev). No array resizing. Poor cache locality.

Text: LinkedList requires {{c1::O(N)}} time for index lookup, but insertion/removal at a known node is {{c2::O(1)}}.
Extra:
Gotcha: Iterating LinkedList using index-based get(i) loops, resulting in O(N^2) complexity.

Details: Backed by doubly-linked nodes (3 references per node: value, next, prev). No array resizing. Poor cache locality.

Text: A legacy synchronized version of ArrayList is {{c1::Vector}}.
Extra:
Why it matters: Synchronizes all methods, guaranteeing thread safety but causing severe contention.

Details: Legacy synchronized resizable array. Obsolete. Doubles capacity when resized (ArrayList grows 1.5x).

Text: Vector is obsolete because all its public methods are {{c1::synchronized}}, causing high performance overhead in single-threaded scenarios.
Extra:
Gotcha: Using Vector in single-threaded applications instead of ArrayList, hurting performance.

Details: Legacy synchronized resizable array. Obsolete. Doubles capacity when resized (ArrayList grows 1.5x).

Text: The legacy LIFO stack class in java.util that extends Vector is {{c1::Stack}}.
Extra:
Why it matters: Violates encapsulation by exposing all Vector methods (like insert at arbitrary index).

Details: Legacy LIFO stack extending Vector. Exposes illegal list methods like insert/remove by index. Use ArrayDeque instead.

Text: Stack is considered poorly designed because it inherits list operations from {{c1::Vector}}, violating {{c2::LIFO}} encapsulation.
Extra:
Gotcha: Using Stack instead of ArrayDeque, which is unsynchronized and enforces clean stack boundaries.

Details: Legacy LIFO stack extending Vector. Exposes illegal list methods like insert/remove by index. Use ArrayDeque instead.

Text: Compared to LinkedList, ArrayList has better CPU cache performance due to {{c1::spatial locality}} of contiguous memory.
Extra:
Why it matters: ArrayList has better cache locality and lower memory overhead; LinkedList has node allocation cost.

Details: ArrayList: O(1) get, O(N) shift, high cache hit. LinkedList: O(N) get, O(1) pointer updates, high GC/memory overhead.

Text: LinkedList has higher memory overhead than ArrayList because it creates a {{c1::node object}} with next/prev references for every element.
Extra:
Gotcha: Assuming LinkedList is always faster for inserts; it is slower if index lookup is required.

Details: ArrayList: O(1) get, O(N) shift, high cache hit. LinkedList: O(N) get, O(1) pointer updates, high GC/memory overhead.

Text: You should use a List when you need to maintain element {{c1::order}} and allow {{c2::duplicate}} values.
Extra:
Why it matters: Provides predictable, ordered storage for elements.

Details: Use List for ordered duplicates. ArrayList is the default. LinkedList only for extensive front insertions/removals.

Text: The default List implementation choice in Java is {{c1::ArrayList}} due to performance and memory efficiency.
Extra:
Gotcha: Choosing LinkedList by default instead of ArrayList, which is generally faster due to cache hits.

Details: Use List for ordered duplicates. ArrayList is the default. LinkedList only for extensive front insertions/removals.

Text: A Set implementation that makes no guarantees about element iteration order is {{c1::HashSet}}.
Extra:
Why it matters: Provides constant-time O(1) operations for basic additions and lookups.

Details: Backed by HashMap. O(1) performance. Unordered. Null key is allowed. Elements must override equals and hashCode.

Text: HashSet uses a {{c1::HashMap}} internally, storing set elements as map {{c2::keys}} with a dummy value object.
Extra:
Gotcha: Expecting HashSet to maintain insertion order, which is not guaranteed.

Details: Backed by HashMap. O(1) performance. Unordered. Null key is allowed. Elements must override equals and hashCode.

Text: A Set implementation that maintains the insertion order of its elements is {{c1::LinkedHashSet}}.
Extra:
Why it matters: Preserves the insertion order of elements during iteration with O(1) performance.

Details: HashMap + doubly-linked list. Maintains insertion order. O(1) operations, slightly slower than HashSet.

Text: LinkedHashSet maintains insertion order by using a {{c1::doubly-linked list}} running through its entries.
Extra:
Gotcha: Assuming it sorts elements; it only preserves insertion order.

Details: HashMap + doubly-linked list. Maintains insertion order. O(1) operations, slightly slower than HashSet.

Text: A Set implementation backed by a Red-Black tree that keeps elements sorted is {{c1::TreeSet}}.
Extra:
Why it matters: Maintains elements in sorted order and provides range-search navigation methods.

Details: Red-Black tree. Sorted order. O(log N) operations. Rejects null. Ignores equals/hashCode, relies on compare/compareTo.

Text: TreeSet rejects {{c1::null}} elements and requires elements to implement {{c2::Comparable}} or use a custom {{c3::Comparator}}.
Extra:
Gotcha: Adding objects that do not implement Comparable or have no Comparator, causing ClassCastException.

Details: Red-Black tree. Sorted order. O(log N) operations. Rejects null. Ignores equals/hashCode, relies on compare/compareTo.

Text: An interface representing a Set sorted in ascending order of its elements is {{c1::SortedSet}}.
Extra:
Why it matters: Provides range views and extreme element retrieval (first, last).

Details: Interface for sorted sets. Defines first(), last(), subSet(), headSet(), tailSet().

Text: SortedSet provides range view operations such as {{c1::subSet()}}, {{c2::headSet()}}, and {{c3::tailSet()}}.
Extra:
Gotcha: Adding null elements, which TreeSet (the main implementation) rejects.

Details: Interface for sorted sets. Defines first(), last(), subSet(), headSet(), tailSet().

Text: An interface extending SortedSet that adds closest-match search methods is {{c1::NavigableSet}}.
Extra:
Why it matters: Allows finding closest matching elements in a sorted collection.

Details: Extends SortedSet. Adds floor(), ceiling(), lower(), higher(), pollFirst(), pollLast(), descendingSet().

Text: In NavigableSet, {{c1::floor()}} returns the greatest element <= e, while {{c2::ceiling()}} returns the least element >= e.
Extra:
Gotcha: Confusing ceiling() (least element >= e) with higher() (least element > e).

Details: Extends SortedSet. Adds floor(), ceiling(), lower(), higher(), pollFirst(), pollLast(), descendingSet().

Text: You should choose a Set implementation when your collection must reject {{c1::duplicate}} elements.
Extra:
Why it matters: Models mathematical set operations like union, intersection, and difference.

Details: Use Set to prevent duplicates. HashSet (default/fast), LinkedHashSet (insertion order), TreeSet (sorted/navigable).

Text: For sorted unique elements, choose {{c1::TreeSet}}; for insertion-ordered uniqueness, choose {{c2::LinkedHashSet}}.
Extra:
Gotcha: Using a Set when element insertion order or positional access is required.

Details: Use Set to prevent duplicates. HashSet (default/fast), LinkedHashSet (insertion order), TreeSet (sorted/navigable).

Text: HashSet checks duplicates using {{c1::hashCode()}} and {{c2::equals()}}, whereas TreeSet uses {{c3::compareTo()}} or {{c4::compare()}}.
Extra:
Why it matters: Ensures correct duplicate rejection depending on the Set implementation.

Details: HashSet: hashCode() matches then equals() returns true. TreeSet: compareTo() or compare() returns 0.

Text: HashSet checks duplicates using hashCode() and equals(), while TreeSet uses {{c1::compareTo()}} or {{c2::compare()}}.
Extra:
Gotcha: Assuming TreeSet uses equals() to check duplicates; it only uses compareTo().

Details: HashSet: hashCode() matches then equals() returns true. TreeSet: compareTo() or compare() returns 0.

Text: If two objects are equal according to equals(), they must return the {{c1::same}} value from {{c2::hashCode()}}.
Extra:
Why it matters: The hashCode contract requires that if x.equals(y), then x.hashCode() == y.hashCode().

Details: Must be overridden together. If equals() is true, hashCode() must match. Mismatched hashes cause collision lookup bugs.

Text: If equals() is overridden without hashCode(), hashing collections will store duplicates because they search in different {{c1::buckets}}.
Extra:
Gotcha: Overriding equals() but not hashCode(), causing duplicate keys/values in HashMaps/HashSets.

Details: Must be overridden together. If equals() is true, hashCode() must match. Mismatched hashes cause collision lookup bugs.

Text: An unbounded queue based on a binary heap that orders elements by priority is {{c1::PriorityQueue}}.
Extra:
Why it matters: Allows retrieving elements according to priority rather than insertion order.

Details: Min-heap based unbounded queue. O(log N) for offer/poll, O(1) for peek. Iterator is unsorted.

Text: Iterating over a PriorityQueue using an iterator does NOT yield sorted elements; you must call {{c1::poll()}} sequentially.
Extra:
Gotcha: Iterating over a PriorityQueue and expecting elements to be sorted; the iterator is unsorted.

Details: Min-heap based unbounded queue. O(log N) for offer/poll, O(1) for peek. Iterator is unsorted.

Text: A resizable-array Deque implementation that is faster than Stack and LinkedList is {{c1::ArrayDeque}}.
Extra:
Why it matters: Faster and more memory-efficient than Stack (as stack) and LinkedList (as queue).

Details: Circular array double-ended queue. Faster than Stack/LinkedList. Rejects nulls. Growable, unsynchronized.

Text: ArrayDeque rejects {{c1::null}} elements and is not thread-safe; for concurrent scenarios, use {{c2::LinkedBlockingDeque}}.
Extra:
Gotcha: Attempting to insert null elements, which ArrayDeque rejects.

Details: Circular array double-ended queue. Faster than Stack/LinkedList. Rejects nulls. Growable, unsynchronized.

Text: When LinkedList is used as a Queue, elements are enqueued using {{c1::offer()}} and dequeued using {{c2::poll()}}.
Extra:
Why it matters: Provides fast O(1) enqueues and dequeues backed by list nodes.

Details: LinkedList implements Queue. Unbounded. Uses node pointer updates for O(1) queue operations. ArrayDeque is generally preferred.

Text: LinkedList acts as an {{c1::unbounded}} queue, which means it will never throw an exception from {{c2::offer()}} due to capacity limits.
Extra:
Gotcha: Using LinkedList when ArrayDeque would be faster and use less memory.

Details: LinkedList implements Queue. Unbounded. Uses node pointer updates for O(1) queue operations. ArrayDeque is generally preferred.

Text: The queue ordering policy where the oldest element is processed first is {{c1::FIFO}}.
Extra:
Why it matters: Standard queue behavior where elements are added to tail and removed from head.

Details: First-In-First-Out. Queue inserts at tail, removes from head. offer() and poll() are standard FIFO methods.

Text: In a standard FIFO queue, elements are added to the {{c1::tail}} and removed from the {{c2::head}}.
Extra:
Gotcha: Expecting Deque.push() to behave in FIFO order; push() is LIFO.

Details: First-In-First-Out. Queue inserts at tail, removes from head. offer() and poll() are standard FIFO methods.

Text: The stack ordering policy where the most recently added element is processed first is {{c1::LIFO}}.
Extra:
Why it matters: Stack behavior where element added last is removed first.

Details: Last-In-First-Out. Stack behavior. Deque uses push() and pop() for LIFO operations.

Text: For LIFO operations, Java developers should use the {{c1::Deque}} interface instead of the legacy {{c2::Stack}} class.
Extra:
Gotcha: Using legacy java.util.Stack instead of Deque implementations.

Details: Last-In-First-Out. Stack behavior. Deque uses push() and pop() for LIFO operations.

Text: A queue that orders its elements according to natural order or a custom Comparator is a {{c1::Priority queue}}.
Extra:
Why it matters: Enables priority-based task execution.

Details: Orders elements by priority using binary heap. Min-priority by default. Rejects nulls.

Text: The head of a PriorityQueue is the {{c1::least}} element according to the specified ordering.
Extra:
Gotcha: Adding non-comparable elements, which triggers ClassCastException.

Details: Orders elements by priority using binary heap. Min-priority by default. Rejects nulls.

Text: An unordered Map implementation based on a hash table is {{c1::HashMap}}.
Extra:
Why it matters: Provides O(1) performance for lookups and insertions.

Details: Hash table bucket array. Java 8+ treeification (list size > 8, capacity >= 64). O(1) avg ops, O(log N) worst.

Text: In HashMap, buckets containing more than 8 elements are treeified into {{c1::Red-Black trees}} if total capacity is at least 64.
Extra:
Gotcha: Using mutable keys whose hashcodes change, causing memory leaks and unreachable values.

Details: Hash table bucket array. Java 8+ treeification (list size > 8, capacity >= 64). O(1) avg ops, O(log N) worst.

Text: A Map implementation that maintains insertion or access order using a doubly-linked list is {{c1::LinkedHashMap}}.
Extra:
Why it matters: Enables building LRU caches using access-order mode.

Details: Extends HashMap. Doubly-linked list preserves order. removeEldestEntry() allows automatic eviction.

Text: To build an LRU cache, LinkedHashMap is constructed with access-order set to {{c1::true}}, overriding {{c2::removeEldestEntry()}}.
Extra:
Gotcha: Thinking LinkedHashMap sorts keys; it only preserves access/insertion order.

Details: Extends HashMap. Doubly-linked list preserves order. removeEldestEntry() allows automatic eviction.

Text: A Map implementation based on a Red-Black tree that keeps keys sorted is {{c1::TreeMap}}.
Extra:
Why it matters: Maintains keys in sorted order and provides navigable lookup methods.

Details: Red-Black tree NavigableMap. Sorted keys. O(log N) operations. Rejects null keys. Compares keys using compare/compareTo.

Text: TreeMap compares keys using {{c1::compareTo()}} or {{c2::compare()}} instead of hashCode() and equals().
Extra:
Gotcha: Inserting null keys, which causes NullPointerException.

Details: Red-Black tree NavigableMap. Sorted keys. O(log N) operations. Rejects null keys. Compares keys using compare/compareTo.

Text: The legacy synchronized map class that rejects null keys and null values is {{c1::Hashtable}}.
Extra:
Why it matters: Guarantees thread safety via coarse locking, which degrades performance.

Details: Legacy synchronized map. Rejects null keys and values. Synchronization on every method. Obsolete.

Text: Hashtable is obsolete because it synchronizes all methods globally; you should use {{c1::ConcurrentHashMap}} for thread safety.
Extra:
Gotcha: Using Hashtable in modern code instead of ConcurrentHashMap.

Details: Legacy synchronized map. Rejects null keys and values. Synchronization on every method. Obsolete.

Text: A highly concurrent, thread-safe Map implementation that locks at node/bucket level is {{c1::ConcurrentHashMap}}.
Extra:
Why it matters: Allows high-concurrency read and write operations without blocking the entire map.

Details: Thread-safe. Node-level locking since Java 8. CAS for empty bins. No global lock. Read operations are lock-free.

Text: ConcurrentHashMap does not throw {{c1::ConcurrentModificationException}} during iteration because it uses weakly consistent iterators.
Extra:
Gotcha: Assuming sequence of operations (containsKey + put) on ConcurrentHashMap is atomic.

Details: Thread-safe. Node-level locking since Java 8. CAS for empty bins. No global lock. Read operations are lock-free.

Text: A Map implementation where keys are wrapped in weak references is {{c1::WeakHashMap}}.
Extra:
Why it matters: Allows keys to be garbage collected when no longer strongly referenced elsewhere.

Details: Keys wrapped in WeakReference. Entry is removed when GC collects the key. Useful for metadata caching.

Text: In WeakHashMap, entries are automatically removed when their {{c1::keys}} are garbage collected.
Extra:
Gotcha: Storing values that contain strong references back to their keys, preventing GC.

Details: Keys wrapped in WeakReference. Entry is removed when GC collects the key. Useful for metadata caching.

Text: A Map implementation that uses reference equality (==) instead of equals() is {{c1::IdentityHashMap}}.
Extra:
Why it matters: Useful for graph algorithms or topology tracking where instance identity matters.

Details: Reference equality (==) comparisons. Uses System.identityHashCode() for hashing. Not a general-purpose Map.

Text: IdentityHashMap compares keys using {{c1::==}} and handles hash codes using {{c2::System.identityHashCode()}}.
Extra:
Gotcha: Using it as a general-purpose map, expecting logical equals() comparisons.

Details: Reference equality (==) comparisons. Uses System.identityHashCode() for hashing. Not a general-purpose Map.

Text: An interface representing a Map sorted in ascending order of its keys is {{c1::SortedMap}}.
Extra:
Why it matters: Provides firstKey(), lastKey(), and range views.

Details: Interface for sorted maps. Provides subMap(), headMap(), tailMap(), firstKey(), lastKey().

Text: SortedMap provides key range operations including {{c1::subMap()}}, {{c2::headMap()}}, and {{c3::tailMap()}}.
Extra:
Gotcha: Inserting non-comparable keys, causing ClassCastException.

Details: Interface for sorted maps. Provides subMap(), headMap(), tailMap(), firstKey(), lastKey().

Text: An interface extending SortedMap with navigation search methods is {{c1::NavigableMap}}.
Extra:
Why it matters: Allows ceilingEntry(), floorEntry(), lowerEntry(), and higherEntry() operations.

Details: Extends SortedMap. Navigation methods: floorEntry, ceilingEntry, lowerKey, higherKey, descendingMap.

Text: In NavigableMap, {{c1::floorEntry()}} returns the entry for the greatest key <= target, while {{c2::lowerEntry()}} is for key < target.
Extra:
Gotcha: Mixing up floorKey() (greatest key <= k) with lowerKey() (greatest key < k).

Details: Extends SortedMap. Navigation methods: floorEntry, ceilingEntry, lowerKey, higherKey, descendingMap.

Text: You should use a Map when you need to store data in {{c1::key-value}} pairs.
Extra:
Why it matters: Allows mapping identifiers to objects.

Details: Use Map for key-value association. HashMap (default/fast), LinkedHashMap (ordering), TreeMap (sorted/navigable).

Text: For O(1) lookups, choose {{c1::HashMap}}; if keys must be sorted, choose {{c2::TreeMap}}.
Extra:
Gotcha: Using key-value lookup when simple Set uniqueness or List ordering is sufficient.

Details: Use Map for key-value association. HashMap (default/fast), LinkedHashMap (ordering), TreeMap (sorted/navigable).

Text: An object that enables forward traversal and safe element removal in a collection is an {{c1::Iterator}}.
Extra:
Why it matters: Provides safe element deletion during traversal via iterator.remove().

Details: Forward traversal of Collection. Methods: hasNext(), next(), remove(). remove() is the only safe way to delete items during loop.

Text: To safely remove an element while iterating a collection, you must call the iterator's own {{c1::remove()}} method.
Extra:
Gotcha: Calling list.remove() inside an active iterator loop instead of iterator.remove().

Details: Forward traversal of Collection. Methods: hasNext(), next(), remove(). remove() is the only safe way to delete items during loop.

Text: An iterator interface that supports bidirectional traversal and modification of Lists is {{c1::ListIterator}}.
Extra:
Why it matters: Enables traversing back and forth, modifying, and adding elements during iteration.

Details: Bidirectional list iterator. Adds hasPrevious(), previous(), set(), add(), nextIndex(), previousIndex().

Text: Unlike standard Iterator, ListIterator supports moving backward using {{c1::hasPrevious()}} and {{c2::previous()}}.
Extra:
Gotcha: Attempting to use ListIterator on Sets or Maps (only works on Lists).

Details: Bidirectional list iterator. Adds hasPrevious(), previous(), set(), add(), nextIndex(), previousIndex().

Text: An iterator that throws ConcurrentModificationException upon detecting modification outside the iterator is {{c1::Fail-fast iterator}}.
Extra:
Why it matters: Prevents non-deterministic behavior under concurrent modification.

Details: Throws ConcurrentModificationException. Tracks modCount vs expectedModCount. ArrayList/HashSet iterators are fail-fast.

Text: Fail-fast iterators detect structural changes by comparing their expectedModCount with the collection's {{c1::modCount}}.
Extra:
Gotcha: Structural modification of a collection using collection methods during a for-each loop.

Details: Throws ConcurrentModificationException. Tracks modCount vs expectedModCount. ArrayList/HashSet iterators are fail-fast.

Text: An iterator that operates on a copy or snapshot, preventing ConcurrentModificationException, is {{c1::Fail-safe iterator}}.
Extra:
Why it matters: Used in concurrent collections to prevent ConcurrentModificationException.

Details: Operates on snapshot/copy (CopyOnWriteArrayList) or weakly consistent view (ConcurrentHashMap). No exception thrown.

Text: Fail-safe iterators used in CopyOnWriteArrayList iterate over a {{c1::snapshot array}}, ignoring subsequent writes.
Extra:
Gotcha: Using snapshot iterators in write-heavy loops, causing excessive garbage collection.

Details: Operates on snapshot/copy (CopyOnWriteArrayList) or weakly consistent view (ConcurrentHashMap). No exception thrown.

Text: The runtime exception thrown when a collection is modified structurally during active iteration is {{c1::ConcurrentModificationException}}.
Extra:
Why it matters: Guards against modification conflicts during traversal.

Details: Runtime exception. Triggered by modCount mismatch. Thrown by next() or remove() in fail-fast iterators.

Text: ConcurrentModificationException is thrown when a collection is modified via its own methods instead of the {{c1::iterator's}} remove().
Extra:
Gotcha: Failing to use Iterator.remove() when removing items from standard lists during loops.

Details: Runtime exception. Triggered by modCount mismatch. Thrown by next() or remove() in fail-fast iterators.

Text: The static utility method used to sort a List in place is {{c1::Collections.sort}}.
Extra:
Why it matters: Uses Timsort to sort lists in O(N log N) time.

Details: Sorts List in place. Uses modified Timsort. stable sort.

Text: Collections.sort internally uses the {{c1::Timsort}} algorithm, which guarantees a time complexity of {{c2::O(N log N)}}.
Extra:
Gotcha: Attempting to sort an unmodifiable list, which throws UnsupportedOperationException.

Details: Sorts List in place. Uses modified Timsort. stable sort.

Text: The static utility method used to reverse the order of elements in a List in place is {{c1::Collections.reverse}}.
Extra:
Why it matters: Reverses elements in place in O(N) time.

Details: Reverses List in place. Swaps elements from ends towards center.

Text: Collections.reverse operates on a List in place, running in {{c1::O(N)}} linear time complexity.
Extra:
Gotcha: Attempting to reverse arrays directly (only works on lists; use Arrays for arrays).

Details: Reverses List in place. Swaps elements from ends towards center.

Text: The static utility method used to randomly permute elements in a List in place is {{c1::Collections.shuffle}}.
Extra:
Why it matters: Useful for generating random permutations.

Details: Randomly permutes List. Uses default Random source. Slow on LinkedList due to positional accesses.

Text: Shuffling a LinkedList using Collections.shuffle is inefficient because it requires {{c1::O(N)}} random access lookups.
Extra:
Gotcha: Calling shuffle on a large LinkedList, which is slow due to O(N) random access.

Details: Randomly permutes List. Uses default Random source. Slow on LinkedList due to positional accesses.

Text: The static utility method that returns the maximum element of a collection is {{c1::Collections.max}}.
Extra:
Why it matters: Iterates through the collection to find the maximum in O(N) time.

Details: Iterates Collection to find max. O(N) complexity. Requires Comparable elements or Comparator.

Text: Collections.max runs in {{c1::O(N)}} linear time because it must inspect every element in the collection.
Extra:
Gotcha: Calling max on a collection containing nulls if the comparator doesn't support nulls.

Details: Iterates Collection to find max. O(N) complexity. Requires Comparable elements or Comparator.

Text: The static utility method that returns the minimum element of a collection is {{c1::Collections.min}}.
Extra:
Why it matters: Iterates through the collection to find the minimum in O(N) time.
